yt_title: How to Pass the WSET Level 3 Blind Tasting: the SAT Step by Step
yt_desc: The WSET Level 3 tasting is a blind tasting of two wines, written up with the Systematic Approach to Tasting (SAT). This study session walks through the method in exam order: appearance, nose, palate and conclusions, with the scales, the aroma families, how to justify quality and readiness for drinking, how to pace two wines, the mistakes that cost marks and a four-week practice plan.

intro.title: Pass the blind tasting with the *systematic approach*
intro.sub: Two wines, one method: describe first, then conclude.
say: The tasting part of WSET Level 3 is a blind tasting of two wines, written up with the Systematic Approach to Tasting, the SAT.
It is marked separately from the theory, with a pass mark of fifty-five percent, so it deserves its own training. Here is the method, step by step.

method.title: Describe first, then conclude
say: The SAT is a method, not a form to fill in. First you describe: appearance,
nose,
and palate. That is where most of the marks sit.
Then you evaluate quality and readiness for drinking, and every judgement must rest on something you have already written.

c1.title: Before the glass
c1.sub: Conditions that make a note reliable
say: Chapter one. Before the glass.

conditions.title: Same routine, every time
items: The **same clean tulip glass**; pour about a quarter
**Good light** and a white surface to judge colour
**No strong smells**; water, crackers, and spit consistently
say: A good note starts before you taste. Use the same clean, tulip-shaped glass every time, and pour about a quarter.
Taste in good light, with a white surface to judge colour.
Avoid perfume, coffee or chewing gum, keep water and plain crackers nearby, and spit consistently. A stable routine means the differences you notice really come from the wine.

c2.title: Appearance
c2.sub: Quick marks that set up the rest of the note
say: Chapter two. Appearance.

appearance.title: Three things to judge
say: Tilt the glass over a white background. Is the wine clear or hazy? And how intense is the colour: how far can you see through it?
Whites run from lemon-green through lemon and gold to amber and brown.
Reds run from purple through ruby and garnet to tawny and brown. An orange-tinged rim in a red often signals development in bottle.

oneterm.title: One term per line
items: Hesitating between two terms? **Choose one**
A range such as *ruby to garnet* **scores nothing**
Keep interpretations for later, and **check them** on the nose and palate
say: One rule applies throughout the note: when you hesitate between two neighbouring terms, choose one.
A range, like ruby to garnet, does not earn the mark, even if the right answer is inside it.
And keep interpretations for later: a deep colour in a white may point to age, oak or a warm climate. Check it on the nose and palate.

c3.title: Nose
say: Chapter three. The nose.

nose.title: Four lines, in order
say: Swirl, then take a short sniff to check condition: clean, or faulty, like the damp cardboard of cork taint.
Then intensity: do the aromas reach you as soon as you lift the glass, or do you have to search?
Then the aroma characteristics. This is where your descriptive range earns marks.
Finally development: tertiary notes mean developing or fully developed; none usually means youthful.

families.title: Work through the families in order

cols.title: Grape and fermentation
items: Floral, green fruit, citrus
Stone, tropical, red, black fruit
Herbaceous, herbal, spice

cols.title: Winemaking
items: Yeast: bread, biscuit
Malolactic: butter, cream
Oak: vanilla, toast, cedar, smoke

cols.title: Ageing
items: Whites: honey, nuts, petrol
Reds: leather, earth, mushroom
Oxidised: toffee, coffee, walnut

families.foot: Specific beats generic: **blackcurrant** > black fruit, **toast** > oak.
say: Move through the aroma families in a fixed order. Primary first, from the grape and fermentation: floral, fruit of every kind, herbaceous and spice.
Secondary, from winemaking: bread and biscuit from yeast, butter from malolactic, vanilla, toast and smoke from oak.
Tertiary, from ageing: honey and nuts in whites, leather, earth and mushroom in reds. And be specific: blackcurrant earns more than black fruit, toast more than oak.

c4.title: Palate
say: Chapter four. The palate.

palate.title: Measure the structure, one at a time
say: On the palate you are measuring. Sweetness is felt at the tip of the tongue; careful, ripe fruit and alcohol can feel sweet in a dry wine.
Acidity makes your mouth water: notice how much saliva gathers after spitting.
Tannin is a texture: it dries and grips the gums.
Alcohol is warmth at the back of the throat.
Body is the overall weight. Don't judge it from flavour intensity: an aromatic wine can still be light.

medium.title: Medium is split in three
medium.foot: Only the medium band is split, because most wines fall there.
say: At Level 3, many scales are refined by splitting medium into medium minus, medium and medium plus.
Only the medium band is split, because that is where most wines fall. It is not five equal parts.

finish.title: Back to flavour
items: Flavour intensity and characteristics usually **echo the nose**
Note any **new families** that appear only in the mouth
**Finish** = pleasant flavours after spitting, not alcohol heat
say: Then return to flavour: intensity and characteristics usually echo the nose, a useful cross-check.
But some notes, like spice or bitterness, only appear in the mouth.
The finish is how long the pleasant flavours last after spitting, not alcohol heat or tannin dryness. Count slowly in your head.

c5.title: Conclusions
c5.sub: Quality and readiness for drinking, with evidence
say: Chapter five. Conclusions.

quality.title: Justify it with four features
cards: Fruit, acid, tannin, alcohol in harmony
items: All four clearly present: likely **very good** or **outstanding**
Balance but limited intensity and a short finish: more likely **acceptable** or **good**
say: Conclusions use only the listed terms, and must follow from your description. For quality, weigh four features. Balance.
Length.
Intensity.
Complexity.
All four clearly present suggests very good or outstanding; balance with limited intensity and a short finish suggests acceptable or good. Name each feature and tie it to your note.

readiness.title: Will it improve?
items: Primary fruit, firm structure, long finish: **can drink now, has potential for ageing**
Tertiary notes, fruit starting to fade: **drink now, not suitable for ageing**
Simple, light and short: **made to be drunk young**
say: Readiness asks whether the wine will improve. Mainly primary fruit, firm structure and a long finish: it can drink now but has potential for ageing.
Tertiary notes and fading fruit: drink now, not suitable for ageing.
Simple, light and short: made to be drunk young. Be consistent: the examiner should be able to predict your conclusion from your description.

examples.title: The conclusion quotes the description

cols.title: Very good
items: Pale lemon-green; lime, green apple, white flowers
High acidity, light body, medium(+) finish
Can drink now, has potential for ageing

cols.title: Outstanding
items: Medium garnet; dried cherry, leather, tobacco, cedar
Ripe soft tannins, full body, long finish
Drink now, not suitable for further ageing

say: A young, cool-climate white: pale lemon-green, lime and green apple, high acidity, light body. Very good, and it has potential for ageing, because acidity and concentrated fruit will carry it.
A mature, warm-climate red: garnet, dried cherry, leather and cedar, soft tannins, long finish. Outstanding, but drink now: the fruit is drying. Each conclusion quotes the description.

c6.title: Exam day
c6.sub: Pacing, mistakes and a four-week plan
say: Chapter six. Exam day.

pacing.title: Work to a plan
items: Look at the **appearance of both wines** first
Complete **wine one** fully: nose, palate, conclusions
Then **wine two**, returning briefly to the nose
**Final check**: one term per line, no ranges, conclusions that match
say: Work to a plan. Look at the appearance of both wines first.
Then complete wine one fully.
Then wine two; a quick return to the nose may reveal extra aromas.
Keep a few minutes to check: one term per line, no ranges, conclusions that match.

mistakes.title: Mistakes that cost marks
head: Mistake
Better habit
rows: Alcohol warmth read as a long finish
say: The costly mistakes. A range between two terms: commit to one. Five descriptors from one family: use all three families.
Generic words like fruity: name the fruit. And alcohol warmth mistaken for a long finish: count only pleasant flavours.

plan.title: Make the method automatic
head: Week
Focus
What to do
rows: Same glass, pour and order; note appearance and nose of every wine
Kitchen exercises; two contrasting wines side by side
Work through the families; aim for specific words
Two wines blind, full notes, then review for consistency
say: A four-week plan. Week one: routine and appearance. Week two: structure, with two contrasting wines side by side.
Week three: descriptors. Week four: two wines blind, timed, then reread your notes with a red pen.

q1.title: You hesitate between ruby and garnet. You write…
q1.expl: Choose **one term**: a range or a combination scores no mark.
say: Quick check. You hesitate between ruby and garnet. What do you write?
The closer single term. A range scores no mark.

q2.title: The finish is…
options: how long pleasant flavours last after spitting
q2.expl: Length is about **pleasant flavours**, not heat or dryness.
say: Question two. What is the finish?
How long the pleasant flavours last after spitting. Not heat, not dryness.

end.title: Practise the theory behind the SAT
end.sub: Questions with explanations on the theory behind the SAT.
say: Now it's your turn. Practise free on thewinegoat.com, with questions and explanations on the theory behind the SAT. Good luck with your exam!
